doc.title: Holly Hofmann interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Discovering the lack of women's role in jazz
summary: Her father's belief that talent alone gets gigs was shattered at Interlochen and college; she still meets discrimination as a woman and a flutist and racial quotas in bands.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: or should I say the lack of the role of women in jazz at that point, because Dad felt that if you played well, it didn’t matter if you were male or female or black or white or what instrument you played, you just would get the gig. And I grew up with that in my mind, and then I got to a certain point where I found out that wasn’t really the case. And that was real hard. It was probably the hardest thing to deal with as a young player. Because I started to realize that there were all sorts of reasons for getting gigs, and a lot of times very little of it had to do with talent.
Is that still something that you feel affects how much work you get? That you’re a woman?

It’s affecting it less and less I’m happy to say. But yes it does. And many times I’m dictated to about rhythm sections, having a certain amount of African-American players and white players, I’m still told many times that flute is not a jazz instrument, it doesn’t belong on this or that. And so there’s discrimination in terms of what instrument I’m playing. Sometimes, unfortunately, still, there’s a group of male promoters that don’t feel women swing, or really belong in the jazz idiom, and that’s getting less and less but it’s still there. And then there is still a strong issue in terms of the African-American community versus the white community as far as you know, who gets the gig in those circumstances too. There’s a group of African-American listeners who feel that they support the African-American musicians simply because they feel it’s their music.
